one_liner: Rust-only columnar, bit-packed serializer; on string-heavy logs it encodes 5-14x faster than prost, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, rmp-serde.
what_it_does: bitcode converts Rust values to a compact byte blob and back. You add #[derive(Encode, Decode)] and call bitcode::encode(&v) -> Vec<u8> and bitcode::decode::<T>(&bytes) -> Result<T, Error>. A reusable bitcode::Buffer keeps allocations between calls, and decode can borrow &str from the input. An optional `serde` feature adds bitcode::serialize/deserialize for existing Serialize/Deserialize types, but it is slower, a little larger, and a different format from the derive encoding. There is no schema file, no codegen and no implementation in any other language, and it cannot read protobuf, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto or MessagePack bytes.
how_it_is_fast: The derive builds a struct-of-arrays encoder tree. Every instance of a field, such as every status code across a Vec of log records, goes into its own column, and each column is packed in one pass at the end. Integer columns get the narrowest byte width that fits the column maximum, optionally after subtracting the column minimum (frame-of-reference). Byte columns with a range under 16 are packed 2-8 values per byte (bools 8 per byte). Lengths take one byte with a 255 escape. Strings become one length column plus one concatenated byte blob, UTF-8-checked once with a SIMD ASCII fast path. Decoding validates every column up front in a `populate` pass, so the per-value decode loop has no bounds or error checks. The loops are written as fixed-size chunks for LLVM auto-vectorization, and short slices are copied with an over-reading fixed-size 'wild copy' instead of memcpy (see gotchas).
when_to_use: Both ends are Rust and built from the same bitcode major version: game or app netcode (including Rust/WASM clients), IPC, internal caches and save files.
Many small records full of strings, small ints, enums and bools. bitcode had the fastest serialize of any crate on the page for 'log' (96.8 µs) and 'minecraft_savedata' (82.0 µs).

Bandwidth or storage matters, with or without compression afterwards. On 'log' it was 703,710 B raw and 227,322 B after zstd, against 884,628 B and 314,959 B for prost; its field-grouped layout is designed to compress well.
no_std targets that have alloc: std is a default feature you can turn off, and CI checks thumbv6m-none-eabi.
Decoding size-capped untrusted input: lengths and UTF-8 are validated, memory allocated stays proportional to input size, and CI runs cargo-fuzz.
when_not_to_use: Cross-language or long-lived data. There is no schema and no non-Rust implementation. The format may change at every major version, and there is no schema evolution: with derive, adding a field or an enum variant must be assumed to break old bytes.

Large arrays of floats or POD structs. On 'mesh', bitcode took 1.23 ms to serialize and 1.26 ms to deserialize. rkyv took 141.7/144.7 µs and wincode 147.9/144.4 µs; FlatBuffers (371 µs) and postcard (413 µs) also serialized faster.

You need zero-copy random access or partial reads. rkyv, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto access a buffer in ns, while bitcode always decodes the whole message, and a streaming API is an open request (issue #6).

Your policy forbids undefined behavior in dependencies. Release builds on x86, x86_64 and aarch64 read past the end of a slice inside the same page; issue #50 is open and PR #51, which would make this opt-in, is unmerged.

Recursive types with derive: not supported, and the compiler fails with a layout cycle. Serde models also fail if they use untagged, internally tagged or adjacently tagged enums, skip_serializing_if/default, or serde_json::Value; these panic with 'type changed'.

integration.dependencies: bytemuck (required); bitcode_derive proc-macro (default `derive` feature); optional: serde, arrayvec, glam, rust_decimal, time, uuid
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.70 for the published 0.6.9 (crates.io rust_version). An unreleased June 2026 commit on main raised rust-version to 1.88.
integration.platforms: Any Rust target with alloc (std optional). CI tests x86_64 and i686 Linux, checks thumbv6m-none-eabi, and runs miri on big-endian powerpc64. The over-reading copy fast path is enabled only in x86, x86_64 and aarch64 release builds.
integration.thread_safety: Buffer is Send + Sync, but encode/decode take &mut self, so use one Buffer per thread. The free encode/decode functions build fresh encoders and decoders per call. Nothing more is documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the serde feature (bitcode::serialize/deserialize) can replace rmp-serde calls on existing serde types, but the bytes are not MessagePack. There is no compatibility with protobuf, FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto data or schemas.

gotchas: The 'wild copy' in src/derive/vec.rs reads a fixed [T; N] block past the end of short slices when the read stays inside the same 4 KiB page. The maintainers acknowledge this as UB on the wiki Security page. It is disabled under miri and debug_assertions, so the tests don't exercise the path that ships in release. PR #51 measured str-vec encode about 28% slower without it (98.5 vs 126.3 µs).
In release builds, Error is a zero-sized type whose message is just 'bitcode error', so you get no hint of which field or column failed. Only debug builds carry a reason string.

Derive (Encode/Decode) and serde (serialize/deserialize) produce different, incompatible bytes for the same type. For example, the serde path drops the SocketAddrV6 flowinfo and scope_id fields. Pick one path per message type.

There is no max-allocation knob, so cap the input slice length yourself. The Security wiki warns that enums with very unbalanced variant sizes, and structs whose fields are all #[bitcode(skip)], can make small inputs allocate a lot.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick bitcode over postcard or serde-zap when both ends are Rust and you want the fastest encode and smallest output on record-shaped data. On 'log' it encoded in 96.8 µs against 366.95 and 135.54 µs, and wrote 703,710 B against 724,953 and 741,295 B. Pick postcard if you need its documented, stable 1.0 wire format; pick rkyv or wincode for float/POD-heavy data or zero-copy access, where on 'mesh' they are about 8x faster than bitcode.
verified_claims_summary: Source: djkoloski/rust_serialization_benchmark, README run of 2026-09-10, 'log' dataset. bitcode 0.6.9 serialized in 96.8 µs, against 731 µs for prost 0.14.4 (encode only), 764 µs for FlatBuffers, 480 µs for capnp and 1.32 ms for rmp-serde. It deserialized into owned structs in 1.15 ms, against 2.68 ms for prost decode and 2.38 ms for rmp-serde, and its output was 703,710 B versus 884,628 B for protobuf. The run used rustc 1.100.0-nightly (LLVM 23.1.1) with LTO, -C target-cpu=native and criterion, with bitcode::Buffer reused across iterations, on a 2-core AMD EPYC 9V74 GitHub Actions VM. capnp and FlatBuffers have no owned deserialize, so only encode is directly comparable with them, and the ranking flips on the float-heavy 'mesh' dataset.
